title: Valid Anagram
directAnswer: If lengths differ, return false. Otherwise count each letter of s (++) and each of t (−−) in a 26-int array; they're anagrams iff every count ends at 0. O(n).

remember.takeaway: Anagram = equal letter frequencies; a 26-array compares them in O(n).
remember.formula: len equal? count[s]++ count[t]--; all zero?

problemStatement: Given two strings `s` and `t` of lowercase letters, return whether `t` is an anagram of `s` (same letters, same counts).
understanding: Two strings are anagrams iff they have identical character counts. A 26-slot count array compares them.

approaches.name: Frequency count (26 array)
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Two strings are anagrams iff they contain the **same letters with the same counts**. A 26-slot count array compares frequencies in O(n): increment for each letter of s, decrement for each of t; they match iff every count ends at 0.

**Why the length check first.** Different lengths can't be anagrams, and the check lets you walk both strings together with one index. It also short-circuits the obvious negatives instantly.

**Why ++ for s and −− for t in one array.** Using a single array, s adds and t subtracts; equal frequencies cancel to all-zeros. This is neater (and one array) versus building two maps and comparing them.

**Why O(1) space.** The count array is fixed at 26 regardless of input size (for lowercase a–z). For full Unicode you'd use a hash map instead. Sorting both strings also works but is O(n log n) — the count array is the O(n) answer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No length check
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without it, 'abc' vs 'ab' may pass a partial comparison; differing lengths can never be anagrams.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
// straight to counting, no guard
int[] c = new int[26]; ...

if (s.length() != t.length()) return false;
